name: Custom PEEK/Medpor jaw implants

lead: Custom jaw implants build a more defined jawline to your own measurements. A surgeon or design team models the implant on a 3D copy of your skull from a CT scan, and it is made in porous polyethylene (Medpor) or the rigid polymer PEEK and placed through the mouth. People use them to add width, height or projection at the jaw angle and ramus, often with chin and cheek implants.

The implant sits on the outside of the bone and adds volume. On forums, members share surgeon lists, post design files and compare planned millimeter dimensions, and custom implants are a common alternative to jaw-moving surgery. Published outcome data for purely cosmetic use is limited.

paras: People typically go through a design stage, planning target proportions with the surgeon before manufacture. The change becomes visible as swelling settles. Forum posters stress careful surgeon selection and design choices.

Risks of any facial implant include infection, displacement, asymmetry and nerve injury, and an implant can need removal. Forum posters note a wider jaw is not always more aesthetic and that some designs produce a rounder rather than more angular jaw.

angle.text: A wider, more defined jawline built to fit your skull. An implant designed from your CT scan adds width or length at the jaw angle and ramus, and the change is visible once swelling settles. Published outcome data for purely cosmetic use is limited.

lead: Custom jaw implants are patient-specific implants fabricated from a CT scan of the patient's facial skeleton to augment the jaw, typically at the gonial angle, the ramus, and sometimes the chin. Two materials are discussed most often in looksmaxxing communities: porous polyethylene, sold under the brand Medpor, and polyetheretherketone (PEEK), a rigid thermoplastic.

The topic is an almost entirely forum-driven one among the sources reviewed. Members of looksmax.org share lists of surgeons they regard as experienced in custom jaw work, post implant design files and discuss target ratios such as bigonial-to-bizygomatic width.[1][2][3] No clinical trial or published case series specifically evaluating custom PEEK or Medpor implants for cosmetic jaw augmentation was found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Jaw angle, ramus, chin, sometimes cheeks
Surgical implant; varies by country and manufacturer

paras: Unlike off-the-shelf silicone or porous polyethylene jaw implants, a custom implant is designed for a single patient from imaging. Forum accounts describe receiving a 3D model file from a surgeon showing lateral projection at the jaw angles, added height to the ramus and anterior chin projection, and asking other members for design feedback before surgery.[3]

Names of surgeons that forum members suggest for wrap-around or custom implants include US-based craniofacial surgeons and a few practitioners in Europe, with discussion focusing on experience with large custom designs.[1]

Forum users describe custom implants as an option for people who want a stronger jawline but do not want or cannot have orthognathic surgery. Threads cover surgeon selection, 3D design, millimeter dimensions and target facial ratios.[1][3]

Design philosophy is a recurring topic. One forum poster argued that many jaw implants produce a round, wide jaw that is not aesthetic and that the ideal is a jaw whose widest point is at the gonial angle and tapers to a sharp chin, combined with cheek implants for hollow cheeks.[2] Another poster with a previous jaw surgery history posted a planned design with specified millimeter projections and asked for help judging chin width and squareness.[3]

No studies found. Published surgical literature on patient-specific implants exists mainly for reconstruction and for facial feminization, and the sources reviewed did not include outcome studies of custom PEEK or Medpor implants used for cosmetic jaw widening.

lore.intro: Custom jaw implants are discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a route to a wider, longer or more angular jaw, with threads about choosing surgeons and critiquing 3D designs.[1][2][3]
